title: A low-temperature entropy source for on-chip true random number generation: universal robustness beyond device quality
authors: Y. Q. Chai, M. Y. Wang, X. N. Feng, L. F. Wei
abstract: True random number generation is a critical capability for fault-tolerant quantum computing at millikelvin temperatures. Yet existing Josephson-junction-based TRNGs all rest on a widely accepted but untested assumption: that reliable entropy extraction requires precisely controlled device parameters. Here we show that this assumption does not always hold. We demonstrate a counterintuitive finding: a single current-biased Josephson junction, regardless of its parameter quality, can serve as a cryptographic-grade true random number generator. To establish the universality of this conclusion, we deliberately selected the most extremely deviated devices from fabrication, with critical currents three orders of magnitude away from theoretical predictions and $I_cR$ products an order of magnitude above conventional values, as the ultimate stress test. Even under these extreme conditions, the raw Shannon entropy reaches 0.9981~bit (99.8\% of the theoretical maximum), with a min-entropy of 0.9271~bit. Using a square-wave pulsed-bias scheme, we tune the switching probability to $P\approx0.5$. After SHA-256 post-processing, the bitstreams pass all 15 NIST SP 800-22 tests under a conservative $m=3$ criterion that is more demanding than the standard recommendation, and this certification holds across the entire 100-700~mK operating window of a dilution refrigerator.
summary: This paper demonstrates that a simple, single Josephson junction can function as a high-quality True Random Number Generator (TRNG) for quantum computing. Crucially, the entropy source is shown to be robust and universal, performing excellently even when the junction's physical parameters are severely degraded. This eliminates the need for stringent, difficult-to-achieve fabrication tolerances for cryogenic quantum hardware.
main_problem: Developing a reliable True Random Number Generator (TRNG) for fault-tolerant quantum computing operating at cryogenic temperatures.
main_result: A single current-biased Josephson junction can serve as a cryptographic-grade TRNG, maintaining high entropy even with severely non-ideal device parameters.
method: The authors used a pulsed-bias scheme on a Josephson junction, analyzed the raw bitstream entropy, and post-processed the data using SHA-256, validating the results against NIST statistical tests.
model_or_system: The physical system is a single current-biased Josephson junction (CBJJ) operating at millikelvin temperatures. The randomness is derived from the stochastic phase-escape dynamics of the junction.
key_observables: Shannon entropy (0.9981 bit), min-entropy (0.9271 bit), and passing all 15 NIST SP 800-22 tests.
important_parameters: Operating temperature range (100–700 mK); switching probability tuned near $P \approx 0.5$; device parameters deviated by up to three orders of magnitude.
main_assumptions: The core assumption challenged is that reliable entropy extraction requires precisely controlled device parameters; the authors show this is not necessary.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the JJ I-V characteristics, the pulsed-bias switching mechanism, and the temperature dependence of the switching probability, while tables summarize NIST test results.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for cryogenic TRNGs, presents the physical model (JJ stochastic switching), details the methodology (pulsed biasing, entropy calculation, SHA-256 extraction), and concludes by demonstrating robustness across extreme device variations.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses hardware requirements for quantum computing by providing a robust, on-chip source of true randomness, which is critical for quantum error correction and computation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Electrical characteristics and stochastic switching behavior of the Josephson junction. (a) I–V characteristic of the JJ. The device exhibits significant underdamped hystere- sis, with normal-state resistance and critical current of 91.5 Ω and 0.672 mA, respectively. (b) Switching current distribu- tion measured at a constant current sweep rate.
FIG. 4. JJ switching probability as a function of pulse amplitude at different temperatures. (a) 0.5 kHz; (b) 1 kHz. The temperature range is 100–700 mK, and the pulse duration is tp = 0.5 ms.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the stochastic voltage switching of a CBJJ under a current pulse. The pulse duration and duty cycle are tp and 0.5, respectively. The pulse amplitude sat- isfies Ipulse < Ic, ensuring that voltage switching occurs only through noise-induced escape. When the CBJJ switches to the voltage state, the voltage across the junction is approx- imately IcR. The voltage threshold Vth for identifying a switching event is therefore set slightly below IcR to mini- mize false identification. The green solid and dashed curves represent the voltage responses of the JJ with and without switching, respectively, during a single current pulse.

FIG. 3. Dependence of JJ switching probability on pulse amplitude. (a) Variation of JJ switching probability with pulse amplitude under 100 mK and 1 kHz conditions. First, a larger step size is used to determine the switching region, then a fine scan is performed at a step length of 0.1 µA. At Ipulse = 0.3512 mA, P = 0.5033 is obtained. (b) Time- domain signals of bias current and JJ output voltage at op- timal pulse amplitude, showing randomly generated “0” and “1” states.
FIG. 5. Raw random bit sequence measured under condi- tions of 100 mK, Ipulse = 0.3512 mA, and 1 kHz square wave pulses. Only the first 100 bits are shown in the figure.
